parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Motivation
parts.text:
The Impact of Motivation represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary arts and culture research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in arts and culture are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Hydrogen as Fuel
parts.text:
Research into hydrogen as fuel has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in science and discovery. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in science and discovery have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Green Hydrogen
parts.text:
The Impact of Green Hydrogen represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary science and discovery research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in science and discovery are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Green Hydrogen
parts.text:

International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 1: Doping in Elite Sport
parts.text:
Research into doping in elite sport has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in transport and infrastructure. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in transport and infrastructure have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Performance Enhancement
parts.text:
The Impact of Performance Enhancement represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary transport and infrastructure research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in transport and infrastructure are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

content.title: Cambridge 9 Test 3 - Writing
content.introduction: Task 1: minimum 150 words, 20 minutes. Task 2: minimum 250 words, 40 minutes.

parts.title: Task 1: Line Graph: Road Traffic Accidents Per 100,000 People 1990-2020
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about line graph: road traffic accidents per 100,000 people 1990-2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

questions.prompt: Planning check: Identify the most noticeable trend in the data.
questions.answerLine: Identify the key trend before writing.

questions.prompt: Overview check: What comparison is most relevant?
questions.answerLine: State the most important comparison in your overview paragraph.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
Some people think that space exploration should change. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.prompt: Planning: Write your thesis statement in one sentence.
questions.answerLine: Draft your thesis before writing the full essay.

questions.prompt: Planning: Name your two main supporting arguments.
questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

content.title: Cambridge 9 Test 3 - Speaking
content.introduction: Speaking test: Part 1 (4-5 min), Part 2 (3-4 min), Part 3 (4-5 min). Speak naturally and extend each answer.

parts.title: Part 1: Introductory Interview
parts.text: The examiner will ask about familiar topics: commuting, travel methods, traffic. Give natural answers of 2-4 sentences each.
tips: Do not memorise scripts — speak naturally and conversationally.
Add one reason or example to each answer.
Avoid one-word responses.

questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: How important is travel methods in your daily life?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: Has your attitude to commuting changed over the years?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: What do you usually do to relax after a busy day?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: Do you think people in your country have enough leisure time?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

parts.title: Part 2: Cue Card
parts.text:
Describe a journey that took longer than expected that was different from what you expected.
You should say:
- what it is
- when and where you experienced it
- what was memorable about it
and explain why it has stayed in your memory.

You have 1 minute to prepare notes and up to 2 minutes to speak.
tips: Use your 1 minute to note 4-5 key words or phrases.
Speak continuously for up to 2 minutes — do not stop early.
End with the 'why' section — it carries significant marks.

questions.answerLine: Self-note.

questions.prompt: Preparation keyword 2 (memorable detail)
questions.answerLine: Self-note.

questions.prompt: Preparation keyword 3 (why it stayed in your memory)
questions.answerLine: Self-note.

parts.title: Part 3: Discussion
parts.text: Broader questions about public transport, car dependency. Develop each answer with an idea, reason, and example or prediction.

questions.answerLine: Discussion question.

questions.answerLine: Discussion question.

content.title: Cambridge 10 Test 1 - Reading
content.introduction: Three academic passages covering Food and Agriculture. 60 minutes, 40 questions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Endangered Languages
parts.text:
Research into endangered languages has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in food and agriculture. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in food and agriculture have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Language Death
parts.text:
The Impact of Language Death represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary food and agriculture research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in food and agriculture are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

parts.title: Passage 1: Endangered Languages
parts.text:

The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. content.title: Cambridge 10 Test 2 - Writing
content.introduction: Task 1: minimum 150 words, 20 minutes. Task 2: minimum 250 words, 40 minutes.

parts.title: Task 1: Bar Chart: Fruit And Vegetable Consumption In Five Countries
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about bar chart: fruit and vegetable consumption in five countries. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

questions.prompt: Planning check: Identify the most noticeable trend in the data.
questions.answerLine: Identify the key trend before writing.

questions.prompt: Overview check: What comparison is most relevant?
questions.answerLine: State the most important comparison in your overview paragraph.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
Young people spend too much time on social media. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.prompt: Planning: Write your thesis statement in one sentence.
questions.answerLine: Draft your thesis before writing the full essay.

questions.prompt: Planning: Name your two main supporting arguments.
questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

content.title: Cambridge 10 Test 2 - Speaking
content.introduction: Speaking test: Part 1 (4-5 min), Part 2 (3-4 min), Part 3 (4-5 min). Speak naturally and extend each answer.

parts.title: Part 1: Introductory Interview
parts.text: The examiner will ask about familiar topics: cooking, food preferences, restaurants. Give natural answers of 2-4 sentences each.
tips: Do not memorise scripts — speak naturally and conversationally.
Add one reason or example to each answer.
Avoid one-word responses.

questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: What do you usually do to relax after a busy day?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: Do you think people in your country have enough leisure time?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

parts.title: Part 2: Cue Card
parts.text:
Describe a meal that was special to you that you remember from your childhood.
You should say:
- what it is
- when and where you experienced it
- what was memorable about it
and explain why it has stayed in your memory.

You have 1 minute to prepare notes and up to 2 minutes to speak.
tips: Use your 1 minute to note 4-5 key words or phrases.
Speak continuously for up to 2 minutes — do not stop early.
End with the 'why' section — it carries significant marks.

parts.title: Passage 1: Endangered Languages
parts.text:
Endangered Languages represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary food and agriculture research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in food and agriculture are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Language Death
parts.text:
Research into the impact of language death has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in food and agriculture. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in food and agriculture have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

content.introduction: Task 1: minimum 150 words, 20 minutes. Task 2: minimum 250 words, 40 minutes.

parts.title: Task 1: Table: Newspaper Readership By Format In Four Countries
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about table: newspaper readership by format in four countries. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

questions.prompt: Planning check: Identify the most noticeable trend in the data.
questions.answerLine: Identify the key trend before writing.

questions.prompt: Overview check: What comparison is most relevant?
questions.answerLine: State the most important comparison in your overview paragraph.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
Some believe criminals should be educated, others believe they should be punished. Discuss.

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.prompt: Planning: Write your thesis statement in one sentence.
questions.answerLine: Draft your thesis before writing the full essay.

questions.prompt: Planning: Name your two main supporting arguments.
questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

parts.title: Part 2: Cue Card
parts.text:
Describe a news story that interested you.
You should say:
- what it is
- when and where you experienced it

parts.title: Passage 1: Animal Ethics in Research
parts.text:
Animal Ethics in Research represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary media and communication research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in media and communication are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Alternatives To Testing
parts.text:
Research into the impact of alternatives to testing has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in media and communication. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in media and communication have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: Match headings to paragraph topics, not isolated details.
MCQ: identify what the question asks before reading options.
Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

parts.title: Passage 1: Animal Ethics in Research
parts.text:
Research into animal ethics in research has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in media and communication. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in media and communication have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Alternatives To Testing

Social dimensions add further complexity. Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Task 1: Table: Newspaper Readership By Format In Four Countries

The diagram/graph below shows information about table: newspaper readership by format in four countries. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:

questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

parts.title: Passage 1: Ocean Plastic Pollution
parts.text:
Ocean Plastic Pollution represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary history and archaeology research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in history and archaeology are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Ocean Plastic Pollution
parts.text:
Research into ocean plastic pollution has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in history and archaeology. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in history and archaeology have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Microplastics
parts.text:
The Impact of Microplastics represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary history and archaeology research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in history and archaeology are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Task 1: Line Graph: Museum Attendance In Three Cities
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about line graph: museum attendance in three cities. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
Some people think that modern approaches should change. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Recidivism
parts.text:
Research into the impact of recidivism has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in psychology and behaviour. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in psychology and behaviour have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: Match headings to paragraph topics, not isolated details.
MCQ: identify what the question asks before reading options.
Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

content.title: Cambridge 13 Test 2 - Reading
content.introduction: Three academic passages covering Psychology and Behaviour. 60 minutes, 40 questions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Prison Reform and Rehabilitation
parts.text:
Research into prison reform and rehabilitation has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in psychology and behaviour. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in psychology and behaviour have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Recidivism
parts.text:
The Impact of Recidivism represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary psychology and behaviour research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in psychology and behaviour are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.text:

parts.title: Passage 1: Prison Reform and Rehabilitation
parts.text:
Research into prison reform and rehabilitation has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in psychology and behaviour. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in psychology and behaviour have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Dark Sky Preservation
parts.text:
Research into dark sky preservation has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in energy and resources. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in energy and resources have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Light Pollution
parts.text:
The Impact of Light Pollution represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary energy and resources research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in energy and resources are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Task 1: Bar Chart: Renewable Energy Production By Type 2000-2020
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about bar chart: renewable energy production by type 2000-2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
Cars should be banned from city centres. To what extent do you agree?

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.prompt: Planning: Write your thesis statement in one sentence.
questions.answerLine: Draft your thesis before writing the full essay.

questions.prompt: Planning: Name your two main supporting arguments.
questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

parts.title: Passage 1: Dark Sky Preservation
parts.text:
Research into dark sky preservation has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in energy and resources. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in energy and resources have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Dark Sky Preservation
parts.text:
Dark Sky Preservation represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary energy and resources research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in energy and resources are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Light Pollution
parts.text:
Research into the impact of light pollution has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in energy and resources. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in energy and resources have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: Match headings to paragraph topics, not isolated details.
MCQ: identify what the question asks before reading options.
Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

parts.title: Task 1: Bar Chart: Renewable Energy Production By Type 2000-2020

The diagram/graph below shows information about bar chart: renewable energy production by type 2000-2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
What are the advantages and disadvantages of cars should be banned from city centres?

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

parts.title: Part 2: Cue Card
parts.text:
Describe a change you made to help the environment that you would recommend to a friend.
You should say:
- what it is
- when and where you experienced it
- what was memorable about it
and explain why it has stayed in your memory.

You have 1 minute to prepare notes and up to 2 minutes to speak.
tips: Use your 1 minute to note 4-5 key words or phrases.
Speak continuously for up to 2 minutes — do not stop early.
End with the 'why' section — it carries significant marks.

parts.title: Passage 1: Social Media and Democracy
parts.text:
Social Media and Democracy represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary sport and exercise research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in sport and exercise are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Disinformation
parts.text:
Research into the impact of disinformation has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in sport and exercise. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in sport and exercise have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Disinformation
parts.text:
The Impact of Disinformation represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary sport and exercise research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in sport and exercise are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Vaccine Hesitancy and Public Health
parts.text:
Vaccine Hesitancy and Public Health represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary language and linguistics research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in language and linguistics are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Mental Health
parts.text:
Research into the impact of mental health has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in language and linguistics. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in language and linguistics have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Part 2: Cue Card
parts.text:
Describe a natural place you have visited that was different from what you expected.

parts.title: Passage 1: The Science of Sleep
parts.text:
The Science of Sleep represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary philosophy and ethics research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in philosophy and ethics are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Memory Consolidation
parts.text:
Research into the impact of memory consolidation has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in philosophy and ethics. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in philosophy and ethics have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in philosophy and ethics. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in philosophy and ethics have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
