content.title: Cambridge 17 Test 2 - Writing
content.introduction: Task 1: minimum 150 words, 20 minutes. Task 2: minimum 250 words, 40 minutes.

parts.title: Task 1: Bar Chart: Percentage Of People Doing Voluntary Work By Age
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about bar chart: percentage of people doing voluntary work by age. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

questions.prompt: Planning check: Identify the most noticeable trend in the data.
questions.answerLine: Identify the key trend before writing.

questions.prompt: Overview check: What comparison is most relevant?
questions.answerLine: State the most important comparison in your overview paragraph.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
It is impossible to protect the environment while also growing economically. Discuss.

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.prompt: Planning: Write your thesis statement in one sentence.
questions.answerLine: Draft your thesis before writing the full essay.

questions.prompt: Planning: Name your two main supporting arguments.
questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

content.title: Cambridge 17 Test 2 - Speaking
content.introduction: Speaking test: Part 1 (4-5 min), Part 2 (3-4 min), Part 3 (4-5 min). Speak naturally and extend each answer.

parts.title: Part 1: Introductory Interview
parts.text: The examiner will ask about familiar topics: technology use, sleep habits, food. Give natural answers of 2-4 sentences each.
tips: Do not memorise scripts — speak naturally and conversationally.
Add one reason or example to each answer.
Avoid one-word responses.

questions.prompt: Tell me about technology use — do you enjoy it?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: How important is sleep habits in your daily life?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: Has your attitude to technology use changed over the years?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: What do you usually do to relax after a busy day?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.prompt: Do you think people in your country have enough leisure time?
questions.answerLine: Personal response.

parts.title: Part 2: Cue Card
parts.text:
Describe a useful app or website that you remember from your childhood.
You should say:
- what it is
- when and where you experienced it
- what was memorable about it
and explain why it has stayed in your memory.

You have 1 minute to prepare notes and up to 2 minutes to speak.
tips: Use your 1 minute to note 4-5 key words or phrases.
Speak continuously for up to 2 minutes — do not stop early.
End with the 'why' section — it carries significant marks.

questions.answerLine: Self-note.

questions.answerLine: Self-note.

questions.answerLine: Self-note.

parts.title: Part 3: Discussion
parts.text: Broader questions about impact of technology on daily life. Develop each answer with an idea, reason, and example or prediction.
tips: Show range with phrases like: 'It depends on...', 'From a different perspective...'
Use hedging language: 'I would argue that...', 'It seems to me that...'
Compare across time, cultures, or social groups where relevant.

questions.answerLine: Discussion question.

questions.prompt: What role should governments play in impact of technology on daily life?
questions.answerLine: Discussion question.

questions.prompt: Do you think attitudes to impact of technology on daily life will change in the future?
questions.answerLine: Discussion question.

questions.prompt: What can individuals do about challenges related to impact of technology on daily life?
questions.answerLine: Discussion question.

content.title: Cambridge 17 Test 3 - Listening
content.introduction: Cambridge-style listening test with 4 sections and 40 questions. Follow strict exam timing for best results.

parts.title: Section 1: Dental Clinic Appointment Booking
parts.text:
A conversation about Dental clinic appointment booking. Listen carefully for names, numbers, and corrected information.

Transcript Focus: Personal details, specific requirements, and factual information confirmed by both speakers.
tips: Watch for correction words: 'actually', 'sorry', 'I mean'.
Write answers exactly as you hear them — no paraphrasing.
Numbers and dates: write immediately when heard.

parts.title: Passage 1: The Science of Sleep
parts.text:
Research into the science of sleep has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in philosophy and ethics. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in philosophy and ethics have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Memory Consolidation
parts.text:
The Impact of Memory Consolidation represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary philosophy and ethics research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in philosophy and ethics are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Smart Cities and Data
parts.text:
Research into smart cities and data has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in wildlife and conservation. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in wildlife and conservation have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

content.title: Cambridge 18 Test 1 - Writing
content.introduction: Task 1: minimum 150 words, 20 minutes. Task 2: minimum 250 words, 40 minutes.

parts.title: Task 1: Diagram: How Solar Panels Generate Electricity
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about diagram: how solar panels generate electricity. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

questions.prompt: Planning check: Identify the most noticeable trend in the data.
questions.answerLine: Identify the key trend before writing.

questions.prompt: Overview check: What comparison is most relevant?
questions.answerLine: State the most important comparison in your overview paragraph.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
Some people say art is essential, others say it is a luxury. Discuss both views.

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.prompt: Planning: Write your thesis statement in one sentence.
questions.answerLine: Draft your thesis before writing the full essay.

questions.prompt: Planning: Name your two main supporting arguments.
questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

content.title: Cambridge 18 Test 1 - Speaking
content.introduction: Speaking test: Part 1 (4-5 min), Part 2 (3-4 min), Part 3 (4-5 min). Speak naturally and extend each answer.

parts.title: Part 1: Introductory Interview
parts.text: The examiner will ask about familiar topics: health, exercise, free time. Give natural answers of 2-4 sentences each.
tips: Do not memorise scripts — speak naturally and conversationally.
Add one reason or example to each answer.
Avoid one-word responses.

questions.answerLine: Personal response.

questions.answerLine: Personal response.

parts.title: Part 2: Cue Card
parts.text:
Describe a time you helped someone.
You should say:
- what it is
- when and where you experienced it
- what was memorable about it
and explain why it has stayed in your memory.

You have 1 minute to prepare notes and up to 2 minutes to speak.
tips: Use your 1 minute to note 4-5 key words or phrases.
Speak continuously for up to 2 minutes — do not stop early.
End with the 'why' section — it carries significant marks.

content.introduction: Three academic passages covering Wildlife and Conservation. 60 minutes, 40 questions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Smart Cities and Data
parts.text:
Research into smart cities and data has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in wildlife and conservation. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in wildlife and conservation have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Urban Sensors
parts.text:
The Impact of Urban Sensors represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary wildlife and conservation research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in wildlife and conservation are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Smart Cities and Data

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Urban Sensors

parts.title: Task 1: Diagram: How Solar Panels Generate Electricity
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about diagram: how solar panels generate electricity. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
What are the advantages and disadvantages of some people say art is essential, others say it is a luxury?

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.

questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

parts.title: Part 2: Cue Card
parts.text:
Describe a time you helped someone that you would recommend to a friend.

- what it is
- when and where you experienced it

content.title: Cambridge 19 Test 2 - Reading
content.introduction: Three academic passages covering Social Change and Inequality. 60 minutes, 40 questions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Microfinance and Poverty
parts.text:
Research into microfinance and poverty has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in social change and inequality. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in social change and inequality have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Small Loans
parts.text:
The Impact of Small Loans represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary social change and inequality research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in social change and inequality are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

Fill-in-blank: the exact word(s) from the passage are usually correct.

parts.title: Passage 1: Microfinance and Poverty
parts.text:
Microfinance and Poverty represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary social change and inequality research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in social change and inequality are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Small Loans
parts.text:
Research into the impact of small loans has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in social change and inequality. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in social change and inequality have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

parts.title: Task 1: Line Graph: Food Price Changes In Three Categories 2000-2020
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about line graph: food price changes in three categories 2000-2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
Some people think that modern approaches should change. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.answerLine: Draft your thesis before writing the full essay.

questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Online Platforms
parts.text:
The Impact of Online Platforms represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary space and exploration research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in space and exploration are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 1: Censorship in the Digital Age
parts.text:
Censorship in the Digital Age represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary space and exploration research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in space and exploration are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.

parts.title: Passage 2: The Impact of Online Platforms
parts.text:
Research into the impact of online platforms has expanded significantly over the past two decades. Scientists and policymakers alike have recognised that understanding this phenomenon is critical to addressing broader challenges in space and exploration. Early studies, conducted primarily in laboratory settings, established foundational principles that have since been refined through field research and longitudinal observation.

The most significant finding concerns the relationship between scale and impact. At local levels, effects are often manageable and reversible. However, when multiplied across global systems, cumulative impacts can reach tipping points that trigger disproportionate and sometimes irreversible change. Researchers working in space and exploration have identified several such thresholds, though the precise conditions under which they are crossed remain subject to ongoing scientific debate.

Policy responses have been mixed. Some governments have implemented proactive frameworks informed by precautionary principles, accepting economic costs in exchange for reduced long-term risk. Others have prioritised short-term economic considerations, delaying regulatory action pending clearer scientific consensus. International cooperation has been inconsistent: while multilateral agreements exist, enforcement mechanisms remain weak and compliance voluntary in many cases.

Economic modelling suggests that early investment in prevention and adaptation is significantly more cost-effective than remediation after harm has occurred. Nevertheless, political short-termism and competing national interests continue to obstruct the level of coordinated action that scientists argue is required.

content.introduction: Task 1: minimum 150 words, 20 minutes. Task 2: minimum 250 words, 40 minutes.

parts.title: Task 1: Bar Chart: Percentage Of Graduates In Stem Fields By Country
parts.text:
The diagram/graph below shows information about bar chart: percentage of graduates in stem fields by country. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
tips: Begin with an overview of the most striking trend or feature.
Group related data — do not describe every single figure.
Use precise comparative language: 'rose sharply', 'remained relatively stable', 'fell significantly'.

parts.title: Task 2: Essay
parts.text:
Humans will travel to Mars within 50 years. Is this a worthwhile goal? Discuss.

Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
tips: Clearly state your position in the introduction.
Each body paragraph should have one main idea + evidence + explanation.
Conclude by restating your view — do not introduce new ideas.

questions.prompt: Planning: Write your thesis statement in one sentence.
questions.answerLine: Draft your thesis before writing the full essay.

questions.prompt: Planning: Name your two main supporting arguments.
questions.answerLine: Identify your two body paragraph topics.

parts.title: Passage 1: Censorship in the Digital Age
parts.text:
Censorship in the Digital Age represents one of the most actively studied questions in contemporary space and exploration research. Historical records trace awareness of the issue to the early twentieth century, though systematic investigation only began in earnest following methodological advances in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, an interdisciplinary community of researchers draws on data from satellite monitoring, field surveys, laboratory experiments, and computational modelling.

A central debate within the field concerns the relative contributions of natural variability and human activity. Long-term datasets spanning multiple centuries reveal cycles of fluctuation that predate industrialisation, complicating causal attribution. However, the speed and scale of change observed since the mid-twentieth century fall outside historical norms in multiple independent datasets, leading the majority of researchers to conclude that anthropogenic factors are the dominant driver of current trends.

Social dimensions add further complexity. Communities most directly affected by changes in space and exploration are often those with the least political and economic power to influence the policies shaping those changes. This asymmetry raises fundamental questions about equity, consent, and responsibility that extend well beyond the technical dimensions of the problem. Advocates argue that effective solutions must address power imbalances alongside technical and scientific challenges.

Looking ahead, scenario modelling projects a range of possible futures depending on the choices made in the coming decade. The most optimistic projections assume coordinated international action and rapid deployment of available technologies. More pessimistic models reflect continued fragmentation of political will and prioritisation of economic growth over sustainability. The gap between best and worst outcomes remains large, underscoring the significance of near-term decisions.
tips: TRUE/FALSE: answer only from the text, not from background knowledge.
Scan for key nouns from each question before reading paragraph by paragraph.
NOT GIVEN: the passage neither confirms nor denies — resist assumptions.
